title: Ancient enemies
hook: 'that's just how i am': Shantideva agrees the enemies are old, and still says they can be driven out
tomorrow: so how does a warrior actually stand against a craving?

segments.voice: Yesterday's riddle, enemies without hands: craving and anger have no hands, no feet, and still they move us, because they borrow our hands. Today, a harder question about them. How long have they been there?
screen: `NO HANDS, NO FEET.` → `HOW LONG HAVE THEY BEEN HERE?`

segments.voice: That's just how I am. People say it about running late, about a short fuse, about biting their nails since second grade. Sometimes it's honest. Sometimes it's a door being quietly locked from the inside. If a habit has lived in you for years, it can feel like furniture, part of the house. Shantideva has an answer, and it isn't the comforting one you might expect. First he agrees: yes, these enemies are very old. Then he says something that sounds impossible.
screen: `THAT'S JUST HOW I AM.` → `A DOOR LOCKED FROM INSIDE.` → `OLD, AND THEN?`

segments.voice: Here's his first move. Ordinary enemies don't last long, he says. These have no beginning and no end in sight. And worse: serve an ordinary enemy and they may turn friendly; serve these, and they only hurt you more. So two views open up, and Buddhists hold both. View one: take the age seriously. Afflictions run deep. Craving has been at work through countless lives, tradition teaches, and anyone who promises it'll vanish by Friday is selling something. Patience with the long road is part of the path. View two: old isn't the same as you. In the Pali suttas, the Buddha calls the mind luminous, stained by defilements that arrive as visitors. A stain on a window isn't the window. The best case for each? The first keeps you humble and steady when the habit comes back. The second keeps you hopeful when it seems permanent. Shantideva stands in both. Ancient, yes. But he still says one can drive them out, because what's built of causes can come apart when the causes change. Old doesn't mean forever. They can go.
screen: `NO BEGINNING, NO END IN SIGHT.` · `VIEW ONE: TAKE THE AGE SERIOUSLY.` · `VIEW TWO: A STAIN ISN'T THE WINDOW.` · `OLD DOESN'T MEAN FOREVER.` · then, large: `THEY CAN GO.`

segments.voice: Choose one old habit you'd like to loosen. Name what you wish for instead, then the moment it usually wins, like the second you sit on the couch. Then make a plan in one sentence: when that moment comes, I'll do this one small thing. Hold the plan in mind for the rest of the sit.
Ancient enemies: the afflictions, old beyond counting, Shantideva says. Old enough to respect, and still not part of the furniture.
Hold on to this: they can go, even the ones that feel like they've always been there. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1473 COUNTS.` → `SHANTIDEVA'S GUIDE · 18 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: SO HOW DOES A WARRIOR ACTUALLY STAND AGAINST A CRAVING?`

howItsDone: Buddhists speak of afflictions both as deep habits carried over many lives, to be worked with patiently, and as passing stains on a mind that is clear by nature; teachers often hold the two together.

match.prompt: two views, one verse — tap the pairs.
pairs: don't last long; can turn friendly
no beginning, no end in sight

myth: if a habit is very old, Buddhism says it's part of who you are

fork.setup: your friend has snapped at people when stressed for as long as anyone remembers. she says 'that's just me, i'll never change.' which reply holds both views?
options: it's deep and old, so be patient with yourself, and it can still loosen.
you're right, a temper that old is just part of who you are.
if you really wanted to, you'd stop snapping by this weekend.
fork.reveal: Shantideva holds both: the enemies are ancient, and they can go. old means patient work, not a life sentence.

original.note: Sanskrit: beginningless, without a first point; used of the afflictions and of the round of rebirth.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old habit is just who you are.
what it means: Shantideva calls the afflictions ancient enemies, and still says they can be driven out.
what a scholar hears: 'beginningless' (anadi) describes the afflictions, while the Pali luminous-mind passage calls the defilements visitors; teachers read both together.
guess: afflictions so old they feel permanent, yet removable
rival families who have feuded for generations
the first sins described at the start of the world

chat.says: painted a little today. but i always quit art things halfway. that's just who i am, right?
options: Quitting halfway is an old habit, not who you are. Old habits can go, slowly.
Yeah, it's your personality. Better to pick smaller projects you can finish.
Just decide you're done quitting tonight, and it'll never happen again.
chat.meaning: Shantideva calls the afflictions ancient, yet says they can be driven out. Old means patient work, not forever.

afflictions.meaning: kleshas: disturbing emotions like craving, anger and confusion

Pali.meaning: the language of the early Theravada Buddhist scriptures

suttas.meaning: the Buddha's discourses, in the Pali scriptures

defilements.meaning: stains on the mind; another English word for kleshas

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 4.33-4.35 (these enemies are long-lasting, without beginning or end; served, other enemies become friendly, these only harm more) and 4.44-4.46 (they can be driven out)
Anguttara Nikaya 1.49-1.52 (the mind is luminous, defiled by incoming defilements)

notes: Debate shape: the two views are both inside Buddhism (the afflictions as deep, beginningless habit to be worked with patiently; the mind as luminous, the defilements as visitors). Neither is ranked. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable presenting them as two emphases most teachers hold together.
'Through countless lives, tradition teaches' is hedged; confirm.
'What's built of causes can come apart when the causes change' is the lesson's gloss on why Shantideva thinks they can go (dependent arising); the explicit argument is in 4.44-4.47. Confirm.
AN 1.49-52 (pabhassara citta) paraphrased; verse numbering varies by edition (1.49-52 in some, 1.51-52 in others).
